entries.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
entries.lesson_core_move: Derive the Fourier-domain output relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ by applying the Fourier transform to the LTI convolution equation and identifying $H(j\omega)$ as the transform of the impulse response.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Introduction to Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output

blocks.text: For one continuous-time LTI system, the output is determined by the impulse response $h(t)$ and the input $x(t)$. In this lesson, we start from the standard time-domain description of that output, not from a new system model.

That convolution equation is the starting point for the frequency-domain derivation. The next steps will apply the Fourier transform to both sides and use the convolution theorem to turn the time-domain convolution into a product.

Here $H(j\omega)$ names the Fourier transform of $h(t)$. So the output spectrum is the input spectrum $X(j\omega)$ multiplied by the system frequency response, and the later steps will show that identification in detail.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Writing the LTI Output as a Convolution

example_content.example_prompt: Given an LTI system with input $x(t)$ and impulse response $h(t)$, write the output $y(t)$ as a convolution integral.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the standard LTI setup: input $x(t)$, impulse response $h(t)$, and output $y(t)$. For an LTI system, the output is written as the convolution of the input with the impulse response.
Expand that convolution into its integral form so the time-domain relation is explicit. Keep the roles of $x(t)$, $h(t)$, and $y(t)$ distinct.

This is the time-domain starting point for the frequency-domain derivation. The next step will transform this same equation; here the only new move is writing the LTI output in standard convolution form.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Applying the Fourier Transform to the Convolution Equation

example_content.example_prompt: Starting from $y(t)=\int_{-\infty}^{\infty}x(\tau)h(t-\tau)\,d\tau$, apply the Fourier transform to both sides and write the transformed relation.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the convolution equation from the previous step. Apply the Fourier transform to both sides of that equation, and name the transformed output spectrum $Y(j\omega)$ without changing the system model.
Keep the right-hand side symbolic at this stage; the convolution theorem will simplify it in the next step. The only new move here is moving the LTI output equation into Fourier form.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Using the Convolution Theorem on the Output Spectrum

example_content.example_prompt: Take the transformed convolution relation from the previous step and simplify it using the convolution theorem.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the transformed convolution relation from the previous step. Apply the convolution theorem to replace the transformed convolution with the product of the two individual transforms, while keeping the same frequency variable $j\omega$.

This is the frequency-domain product form of the output relation. The only new move here is using the convolution theorem to replace the transformed convolution with a product of spectra, without yet renaming the transform of $h(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Identifying $H(j\omega)$ as the Transform of $h(t)$

example_content.example_prompt: Given the impulse response $h(t)$, identify its Fourier transform $H(j\omega)$ and substitute it into the output relation.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the transform of the impulse response from the previous step. Name that transform as $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$, then substitute it into the frequency-domain product so the system term is written with standard notation.
This is the frequency-response notation for the LTI system. The input spectrum stays $X(j\omega)$, the output spectrum stays $Y(j\omega)$, and the system contribution is now isolated as $H(j\omega)$.

sections.lesson_title: Fourier Transform of an LTI System Output
sections.section_title: Deriving $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$

example_content.example_prompt: Starting from the convolution equation and the definition of $H(j\omega)$, derive the final relation $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the full derivation from the time-domain LTI model to the frequency-domain output formula. Start with the convolution expression, transform both sides, use the convolution theorem, and then replace $\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$ with $H(j\omega)$.
This completes the lesson's core move. The output spectrum is the input spectrum multiplied by the system frequency response, so the final relation is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the time-domain output of an LTI system by forming $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, simplifying the product, and applying the inverse Fourier transform.

sections.lesson_title: Finding Output with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Introduction to Finding Output with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$

blocks.text: When an LTI system is described in the frequency domain, the output is found by staying in $j\omega$ until the output spectrum is formed. If the input spectrum is $X(j\omega)$ and the system response is $H(j\omega)$, then the output spectrum is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

$H(j\omega)$ comes from the impulse response $h(t)$, so the system is already represented by a transform pair. The only new work is to identify the two factors, multiply them, and simplify the product only as much as needed.

The full procedure is always the same: read off $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$, form $Y(j\omega)$, simplify the product if that makes the inverse transform easier, and then apply the inverse Fourier transform to recover $y(t)$. Keep the first pass small so the theorem attaches to one repeatable algebraic move before the lesson becomes more abstract.

sections.lesson_title: Finding Output with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Forming $Y(j\omega)$ from $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$

example_content.example_prompt: Given $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{j\omega+1}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{2}{j\omega+3}$, form $Y(j\omega)$ in product form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the input spectrum $X(j\omega)$ and the system response $H(j\omega)$ are already given, so the only job is to multiply them using the frequency-domain LTI rule $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$. Substitute the two expressions exactly as they are, with no cancellation yet.
This is the correct output spectrum in product form. Leave both factors visible so the next step can simplify the product before moving on to the inverse Fourier transform.

sections.lesson_title: Finding Output with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Simplifying the Frequency-Domain Product

example_content.example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2(j\omega+4)}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+2)}\cdot\frac{j\omega+1}{j\omega+4}$, simplify the product before inversion.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that the product already contains a factor that appears in both the numerator and denominator, so the job is to simplify $Y(j\omega)$ before inversion. Start from the product exactly as formed in the previous step and keep the notation unchanged.
Now cancel the shared factors $(j\omega+1)$ and $(j\omega+4)$. After the cancellation, the spectrum is much simpler and is ready to match a standard inverse-transform pair.
This reduced form is the correct answer for this step. Keep the output in this transform-ready shape so the next step can recover $y(t)$ without carrying the canceled factors any farther.

sections.lesson_title: Finding Output with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Inverting $Y(j\omega)$ Using a Known Transform Pair

example_content.example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2}{j\omega+2}$, use the standard pair for $e^{-at}u(t)$ to find $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the single factor $j\omega+2$ in the denominator. That matches a standard causal exponential pair, so the job here is to recognize the form and read off the time-domain signal directly.
The constant $2$ stays outside the pair, and the value $2$ in the denominator becomes the decay rate. The inverse transform gives the output $y(t)=2e^{-2t}u(t)$ with no extra algebra.

sections.lesson_title: Finding Output with $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$
sections.section_title: Finding $y(t)$ from a Decomposed Frequency-Domain Product

example_content.example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2}{(j\omega+1)(j\omega+3)}$, decompose it into standard terms and find $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the product of two first-order factors in the denominator. That means split $Y(j\omega)$ into a sum of standard single-pole terms, then invert each term separately.
Clear the denominators to get $2=A(j\omega+3)+B(j\omega+1)$. Matching the poles gives $A=1$ and $B=-1$, so the spectrum becomes a difference of two standard causal-exponential pairs.
This is the output signal. The decomposition lets linearity handle the inverse transform term by term, so the final answer is just the sum of the two time-domain pieces.

entries.lesson_title: Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
entries.lesson_core_move: Choose between direct convolution and frequency-domain multiplication by comparing the time-domain overlap integral with the transform-pair, multiplication, and inverse-transform workload.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
sections.section_title: Introduction to Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication

blocks.text: For a continuous-time LTI system, there are two valid output routes: direct convolution in time and multiplication in frequency. Use this step to compare the work each route requires before you choose a method.

The decision is about workload, not about which formula is more correct. In the time-domain route, you find the overlap interval, set the bounds, and evaluate the integral piecewise if the overlap changes with $t$.

In the frequency-domain route, you look up or derive transform pairs, multiply the spectra, and then check whether the inverse transform is immediate or messy. Start with a case where the overlap is one simple interval and the frequency-domain route is also available, so the choice comes from counting steps instead of from hidden tricks.
Choose the shorter symbolic path. Let a difficult overlap, a hard transform lookup, or a messy inverse transform tip the decision toward the other method.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
sections.section_title: Comparing Workloads When the Time-Domain Overlap Is Simple

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, decide whether direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication is the shorter path for finding $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is compact support: both signals are short rectangular pulses, so the decision is about which symbolic route has less work, not about which formula is more valid.
The time-domain route is short because the overlap is just one simple interval at a time. You set the convolution bounds once, integrate a simple product, and avoid extra transform bookkeeping.

The frequency-domain route is longer here because you still need both transform pairs, the product $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, and an inverse transform to get back to $y(t)$. That is more symbolic work than the single overlap integral.

So the shorter path is direct convolution. The important point is not that convolution always wins, but that a simple overlap can make the time-domain integral cheaper than lookup, multiplication, and inversion.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
sections.section_title: Comparing Workloads When Transform Pairs Are Available

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$, decide whether direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication is the shorter path for finding $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is a pair of standard causal exponentials. Because the transform pairs are already available, the decision is about which route needs fewer symbolic steps overall.

The time-domain route would still require the full convolution setup: find the overlap interval, write the integral, and simplify the result. That is valid, but it is not the shortest route when the supports are already easy to describe and the transform tables are ready to use.

The frequency-domain route starts from those known pairs, multiplies them to get $Y(j\omega)$, and then uses a routine inverse transform. Here the lookup plus product is shorter than the overlap integral, so frequency-domain multiplication is the better choice.

So the correct decision is to use frequency-domain multiplication. The key point is that the method choice comes from counting the work: when the transform pairs are already known, the frequency-domain path can be cheaper than direct convolution.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
sections.section_title: Comparing Workloads When the Inverse Transform Is Hard

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, decide whether direct convolution or frequency-domain multiplication is the shorter path for finding $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite pulse feeding a causal exponential. Both routes are available, so the choice comes down to symbolic workload, not to whether the transforms exist.
The direct-convolution route stays inside one finite overlap interval, so it is just one manageable integral to set up and simplify.

The frequency-domain route also starts from known pairs, but the product is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)=\frac{1-e^{-j\omega}}{j\omega(1+j\omega)}$. That product does not collapse to a single simple inverse-transform pair, so the inverse step needs extra algebra before $y(t)$ appears.

So the shorter path here is direct convolution. The important comparison is not just whether transform pairs are available, but whether the inverse transform is simple enough to justify switching domains.

sections.lesson_title: Comparing Direct Convolution and Frequency-Domain Multiplication
sections.section_title: Choosing the Easier Output Method from Both Workflows

example_content.example_prompt: For $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, compare direct convolution and frequency-domain multiplication and choose the easier route for finding $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a finite pulse, $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$, feeding a causal exponential, $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$. Both routes are available, so the decision is about the total symbolic workload.

The direct-convolution route stays inside one finite overlap interval. Once the overlap is identified, the result comes from a single piecewise integral and its simplification, so the time-domain path stays compact.
The frequency-domain route starts from known pairs, but it adds two lookups, a product, and then an inverse transform that does not fall out of one table entry.

That product can be simplified, but only after extra algebra such as partial fractions or a shift decomposition. So even though the frequency-domain route is available, it is not the shorter one here.

The easier method is direct convolution. The decision rule is to count the whole workflow, not just the first familiar step: here the finite overlap integral is cheaper than transform lookup, multiplication, and inversion.

entries.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the output of an LTI system for a periodic input by scaling each Fourier-series harmonic coefficient by the frequency response at that harmonic, $Y_k=H(jk\omega_0)X_k$.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Introduction to Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System

blocks.text: A periodic input is handled one harmonic at a time. Start by writing the Fourier-series form of the input, where each coefficient $X_k$ belongs to the harmonic at frequency $k\omega_0$.

For a single complex exponential $e^{j\omega t}$, an LTI system keeps the same frequency and scales the signal by $H(j\omega)$. So the harmonic with index $k$ keeps its index and picks up the factor $H(jk\omega_0)$.
The DC term is just the $k=0$ harmonic, so it uses $H(0)$. Positive and negative harmonics follow the same rule, with each coefficient scaled by the response value at its own frequency.
The operational takeaway is simple: compute each $Y_k$ separately, then rebuild the periodic output from the scaled coefficients.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Scaling One Fourier-Series Harmonic by $H(jk\omega_0)$

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic input has one nonzero harmonic coefficient $X_2=3-2j$, and the system response at that harmonic is $H(j2\omega_0)=1+j$. Find the output coefficient $Y_2$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a single Fourier-series harmonic with index $k=2$. Use the harmonic-scaling rule from the tutorial: keep the same harmonic index and change only the coefficient.
Here the input coefficient is $X_2=3-2j$ and the matching response value is $H(j2\omega_0)=1+j$. Substitute those values directly into $Y_k=H(jk\omega_0)X_k$.
So the output coefficient is $Y_2=5+j$. The harmonic frequency itself does not change; only the coefficient attached to the $k=2$ harmonic changes.
That is the pattern to reuse for every other harmonic: match the index, multiply by the response value at that frequency, and simplify the product.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Computing Output Coefficients for Several Harmonics

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic input has coefficients $X_{-1}=1+j$, $X_0=2$, and $X_1=1-j$, and the system response values are $H(-j\omega_0)=2$, $H(0)=\tfrac12$, and $H(j\omega_0)=1-j$. Find $Y_{-1}$, $Y_0$, and $Y_1$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a small Fourier-series table with one DC term and two side harmonics. Match each harmonic index to its own response value before multiplying.
Use the same scaling rule for each index: $Y_k=H(jk\omega_0)X_k$. Here that means one computation for $k=-1$, one for $k=0$, and one for $k=1$.
So the output coefficients are $Y_{-1}=2+2j$, $Y_0=1$, and $Y_1=-2j$. Each harmonic keeps its index; only the coefficient changes.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Scaling the DC Component with $H(0)$

example_content.example_prompt: A periodic input has DC coefficient $X_0=4$ and the system has $H(0)=\frac12$. Find the output DC coefficient $Y_0$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the $k=0$ harmonic, or DC term. For periodic inputs, the DC term follows the same harmonic-scaling rule as every other coefficient.
Here the input has $X_0=4$ and the system gain at zero frequency is $H(0)=\frac12$. Write the output coefficient as $Y_0=H(0)X_0$.
So the output DC coefficient is $Y_0=2$. The harmonic index stays $k=0$; only the coefficient is scaled.
This is the same move you will reuse whenever a periodic input has a nonzero DC term: match $k=0$, multiply by $H(0)$, and simplify.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Scaling Positive and Negative Harmonic Pairs

example_content.example_prompt: A real periodic input has $X_1=2-j$ and $X_{-1}=2+j$, while the system response is $H(j\omega_0)=1-j$ and $H(-j\omega_0)=1+j$. Find $Y_1$ and $Y_{-1}$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a positive/negative harmonic pair at $k=1$ and $k=-1$. Treat each sign separately and match each coefficient to its own response value.
Here $X_1=2-j$ matches $H(j\omega_0)=1-j$, and $X_{-1}=2+j$ matches $H(-j\omega_0)=1+j$. Write the two coefficient relations directly.
So the output pair is $Y_1=1-3j$ and $Y_{-1}=1+3j$. Each sign of $k$ uses its own response value; the index does not get swapped.
For a real input, the positive and negative harmonics stay conjugate after scaling. The reusable move is to match $k$ with $H(jk\omega_0)$ before multiplying.

sections.lesson_title: Periodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Reconstructing the Periodic Output from Scaled Coefficients

example_content.example_prompt: Given scaled coefficients $Y_{-1}=1+j$, $Y_0=2$, and $Y_1=1-j$, write the output $y(t)$ as a Fourier series and, if helpful, convert the conjugate pair into a real sinusoidal form.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a short list of output coefficients. Reconstruct the periodic output by placing each coefficient back on its harmonic, then group the conjugate pair if you want a real-signal form.
Here the scaled coefficients are $Y_{-1}=1+j$, $Y_0=2$, and $Y_1=1-j$. Substitute them into the Fourier-series synthesis formula for $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.latex: \begin{aligned}y(t) &= \sum_{k=-1}^{1} Y_k e^{jk\omega_0 t} \\ &= Y_{-1}e^{-j\omega_0 t}+Y_0+Y_1e^{j\omega_0 t} \\ &= (1+j)e^{-j\omega_0 t}+2+(1-j)e^{j\omega_0 t} \\ &= 2+2\cos(\omega_0 t)+2\sin(\omega_0 t)\end{aligned}

explanation_blocks.text: So the reconstructed output can be written as $y(t)=(1+j)e^{-j\omega_0 t}+2+(1-j)e^{j\omega_0 t}$, or equivalently as $y(t)=2+2\cos(\omega_0 t)+2\sin(\omega_0 t)$. The coefficients are back in the signal, and the harmonic indices are unchanged.
This closes the workflow: scale each Fourier coefficient, then rebuild $y(t)$ from the scaled coefficients using the same harmonic basis.

entries.lesson_title: Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System
entries.lesson_core_move: Compute the output of an LTI system for an aperiodic input by transforming the input to $X(j\omega)$, multiplying by $H(j\omega)$, and inverting $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ to recover $y(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Introduction to Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System

blocks.text: For an aperiodic input through an LTI system, start by recognizing the convolution relation $y(t)=x(t)*h(t)$. The frequency-domain method keeps the work out of the convolution integral and turns that convolution into multiplication.

Define $X(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{x(t)\}$ and $H(j\omega)=\mathcal{F}\{h(t)\}$. Once those spectra are identified, the output spectrum is $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$, so the workflow is transform, multiply, simplify, and invert.

In the base case, use a simple causal exponential input and a simple causal first-order impulse response. Both transforms come from the table, so you can write the product explicitly before doing any inversion.

After the product is simplified into a standard transform pair or a form that can be matched with partial fractions, recover the output with the inverse Fourier transform. The final answer should keep the expected causal shape of the original input-system pair.
Keep the checklist fixed: transform the input and impulse response, multiply to form $Y(j\omega)$, simplify until the inverse pair is visible, and invert to get $y(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding Output from a Direct Aperiodic Transform Pair

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, find $y(t)$ using the Fourier transform method.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a causal exponential input together with a causal first-order impulse response, so the direct path is to read both spectra from the transform table and stay in the frequency domain.
Multiply the spectra to form the output spectrum. This is the only algebraic step before the inverse transform.
Rewrite the product in a form that matches standard inverse-transform pairs. Here, partial fractions give a difference of two simple first-order terms.
Invert each term and combine the result in time domain. The output stays causal, and the inverse transform produces the expected difference of exponentials.

The direct transform-pair workflow is therefore table lookup, multiply, simplify, and invert. For this aperiodic input and first-order LTI system, that gives the causal output $y(t)=\big(e^{-t}-e^{-2t}\big)u(t)$.

sections.lesson_title: Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Multiplying an Aperiodic Input Spectrum by $H(j\omega)$

example_content.example_prompt: Given $X(j\omega)=\frac{1}{2+j\omega}$ and $H(j\omega)=\frac{2+j\omega}{3+j\omega}$, find $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is that both the input and the system are already given in the frequency domain, so the task is to form $Y(j\omega)=X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$ and simplify the product before inverting.
The factor $2+j\omega$ cancels immediately. That leaves a single first-order term, which matches a standard inverse-transform pair.
Now invert the simplified spectrum. Since $\frac{1}{3+j\omega}$ is the transform of a causal exponential, the output is the corresponding decaying time signal.
The pattern to copy is multiply first, cancel any common factor, then invert the reduced spectrum. The time-domain answer comes only after the product has been simplified to a known pair.

sections.lesson_title: Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Recovering $y(t)$ from a Simplified Frequency-Domain Product

example_content.example_prompt: Given $Y(j\omega)=\frac{2}{(1+j\omega)(3+j\omega)}$, find $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a rational spectrum with two simple poles, so the job is to split it into standard first-order terms and invert each one separately.
Write the product as a partial-fraction sum with unknown coefficients, then solve for the values that reproduce the numerator.
Matching coefficients gives $A=1$ and $B=-1$, so the spectrum becomes a difference of two standard causal terms.
Now invert term by term. Each fraction matches the causal exponential pair, and the time-domain result is the difference of the two decays.
The pattern to copy is recognize the poles, decompose the rational function, and invert each first-order term directly. The unit step stays attached to preserve causality.

sections.lesson_title: Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding Output for a Shifted Aperiodic Input

example_content.example_prompt: If $x(t)=e^{-(t-2)}u(t-2)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, find $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a delayed exponential, so treat $x(t)$ as the base signal $x_0(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ shifted by 2. The Fourier shift property contributes the factor $e^{-j2\omega}$ to $X(j\omega)$.
Multiply the spectra and keep the shift factor visible. The delay does not disappear during the product; it stays attached to the whole frequency-domain expression.
The unshifted inverse pair is $\frac{1}{(1+j\omega)^2}\leftrightarrow t e^{-t}u(t)$. Apply the delay factor to that base result instead of rebuilding the algebra from scratch.
The delay factor shifts the whole output by 2, so the time-domain response is the base output evaluated at $t-2$ and multiplied by $u(t-2)$.
The pattern to copy is base exponential, shift factor, multiply in frequency domain, then delay the known time-domain result. The shift moves the entire response, not just the exponential term.

sections.lesson_title: Aperiodic Inputs Through an LTI System
sections.section_title: Finding Output for a Sum of Aperiodic Inputs

example_content.example_prompt: Given $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)+e^{-2t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$, find $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is a sum of two causal exponentials, so split $x(t)$ into two component signals and use linearity to process each one through the same LTI system.
Multiply each input spectrum by the same $H(j\omega)$. The two components stay separate until the very end, so each output term can be inverted on its own.
Invert each product using the same transform pairs from the earlier examples. The first term gives the repeated-pole response, and the second term gives the difference of two exponentials.
Add the component outputs to recover the full response, then combine like terms if desired. Superposition applies after inversion just as it did before the transform.

The pattern to copy is split, solve each part through the same system, and then recombine the outputs. For a sum of aperiodic inputs, linearity keeps the work organized and the final expression causal.

entries.lesson_core_move: Select and apply either convolution or frequency-response multiplication to compute a continuous-time LTI system output from the input type and available system description.

sections.lesson_title: Convolution and Frequency-Response Approaches
sections.section_title: Introduction to Convolution and Frequency-Response Approaches

blocks.text: To find the output $y(t)$ of a continuous-time LTI system, first compare the two standard routes: direct convolution in time or multiplication in frequency.

Use direct convolution when $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ are easy to overlap and the integral stays short. In the simple rectangle-through-rectangle base case from the outline, the overlap interval is short enough that the time-domain route is the cleaner first choice.

Use frequency-response multiplication when $X(j\omega)$ and $H(j\omega)$ come from standard transform pairs or are easy to form by linearity. In that case, the product is usually shorter than writing out and simplifying a piecewise convolution.
Compare overlap complexity, availability of transform pairs, and inverse-transform difficulty. Pick the route that reaches $y(t)$ with the least case-splitting and the cleanest final algebra.

sections.lesson_title: Convolution and Frequency-Response Approaches
sections.section_title: Choosing Direct Convolution from Simple Overlap Bounds

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=u(t)-u(t-2)$ by direct convolution; the overlap interval is short and the time-domain route is the cleanest choice.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is simple: both $x(t)$ and $h(t)$ are finite-duration rectangles, so the overlap bounds are easy to track. That makes direct convolution the shortest path to $y(t)$.

Since $x(\tau)=1$ on $0\le \tau<1$ and $h(t-\tau)=1$ when $t-2\le \tau<t$, the integrand is 1 only where those two intervals overlap. So the output is determined by the overlap of $[0,1]$ and $[t-2,t]$.
That overlap has length $t$ for $0\le t<1$, length $1$ for $1\le t<2$, and length $3-t$ for $2\le t<3$. Outside that range, the intervals do not overlap and the output is 0.

explanation_blocks.latex: y(t)=\begin{cases}0,& t<0\\ t,& 0\le t<1\\ 1,& 1\le t<2\\ 3-t,& 2\le t<3\\ 0,& t\ge 3\end{cases}

explanation_blocks.text: This is the direct-convolution advantage in the simple overlap case: the bounds alone determine the piecewise answer, and no frequency-domain work is needed.

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ and $h(t)=e^{-2t}u(t)$ by multiplying the known transform pairs and inverting the product.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue here is the causal exponential form: both $e^{-t}u(t)$ and $e^{-2t}u(t)$ are standard transform pairs, so frequency-response multiplication is the shorter path to $y(t)$.
Multiply the transform pairs to form $Y(j\omega)$. Because each factor already has a standard inverse pair, the frequency-domain route avoids the time-domain overlap integral entirely.
Now invert term by term using the standard causal exponential pairs. Keeping the $u(t)$ factors makes the time-domain output causal, which matches the original signals.
This is the frequency-response advantage in the known-pair case: the transform table and a short algebraic simplification give $y(t)$ faster than a direct convolution calculation.

sections.section_title: Choosing Frequency-Response Multiplication to Avoid Piecewise Convolution

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)+u(t-2)-u(t-3)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ by using frequency-response multiplication rather than a multi-interval convolution.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the repeated pulse structure in $x(t)$. A direct convolution would split into several overlap cases, so the shorter route is to rewrite the input as shifted copies of one base pulse and use linearity plus the shift property.

Now use the known frequency response of the causal exponential system. Because the same base pulse appears twice, the transform work stays compact and the shift factor carries straight through the product.
Let $g(t)$ be the output for the single pulse $p(t)$. The factor $e^{-j2\omega}$ becomes a time shift, so the second pulse contributes a copy of the same response delayed by 2.

This is the frequency-response advantage in the multi-shift case: the repeated pulse train turns into one base response plus one shift, instead of several convolution intervals and piecewise overlap calculations.

sections.section_title: Choosing Direct Convolution to Avoid Difficult Inverse Transforms

example_content.example_prompt: Compute $y(t)$ for $x(t)=u(t)-u(t-1)$ and $h(t)=e^{-t}u(t)$ by direct convolution because the time-domain integral is shorter than inverting $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the single rectangular pulse in $x(t)$. Here the time-domain route is shorter because the overlap is easy to track, while the frequency-domain product would still need more inverse-transform work.
Because $x(\tau)$ is nonzero only on $0\le \tau<1$ and $h(t-\tau)$ is nonzero only when $\tau\le t$, the overlap changes only at $t=0$ and $t=1$. That gives one zero case and two short causal cases.
So the direct-convolution answer is piecewise only where the overlap changes. That is shorter than inverting $X(j\omega)H(j\omega)=\frac{1-e^{-j\omega}}{j\omega(1+j\omega)}$.

example_content.example_prompt: For $H(j\omega)=\frac{1}{1+j\omega}$ and $x(t)=e^{-t}u(t)+u(t)-u(t-1)$, choose the shorter approach and compute $y(t)$.

explanation_blocks.text: The cue is the mixed input: one causal exponential and one shifted rectangle. Each piece has a standard transform pair, so frequency-response multiplication is the shorter path to $y(t)$.
Use linearity to multiply each input component by $H(j\omega)$. That gives one squared-denominator term from the exponential piece and one shifted pulse-response term from the rectangle.
Invert the two standard factors separately. The squared denominator gives $t e^{-t}u(t)$, and the pulse term is the same unit-pulse response from the previous step.

That finishes the capstone: the selection rule points to frequency-response multiplication, and the full output comes from combining the transformed pieces without setting up a separate time-domain convolution for each term.
